Abstract
Introduction
While AI-generated training recommendations may enhance the scientific rigor of competitive sports training, their use may also be associated with athletes’ autonomy in interpreting bodily states and making training decisions. Drawing on cognitive offloading theory, self-determination theory, and the appropriate reliance framework, this study examined a serial association model linking AI training recommendation dependence, body signal outsourcing tendency, reduced sense of self-regulation, training decision hesitation, and reduced training self-efficacy.
Methods
Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 381 athletes. The hypothesized relationships were tested using structural equation modeling, bootstrap analyses of indirect associations, and multigroup analyses comparing athletes in physical-dominant and skill-dominant sports.
Results
AI training recommendation dependence was significantly and positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency, which was, in turn, positively associated with a reduced sense of self-regulation. A reduced sense of self-regulation was positively associated with training decision hesitation, which was further positively associated with reduced training self-efficacy. Bootstrap analyses identified a significant serial indirect association between AI training recommendation dependence and reduced training self-efficacy through body signal outsourcing tendency, reduced sense of self-regulation, and training decision hesitation. Multigroup analyses further indicated that the positive association between AI training recommendation dependence and body signal outsourcing tendency was stronger among athletes in physical-dominant sports than among those in skill-dominant sports.
Discussion
The findings reveal a continuous pattern of statistical associations linking AI training recommendation dependence with body signal outsourcing tendency, reduced sense of self-regulation, training decision hesitation, and reduced training self-efficacy. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining athletes’ bodily awareness and capacity for autonomous decision-making when integrating AI-generated recommendations into competitive sports training.
Keywords:
AI training recommendation dependence, body signal outsourcing, sense of self-regulation, training decision hesitation, training self-efficacy

The most defensible model emerging from the evidence is human-AI collaboration, in which ML enhances precision and consistency in data interpretation, while coaches retain responsibility for contextual judgement, ethical decision-making, and athlete-centred care.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/bios16020097\", \"pmid\": \"41744715\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12938206\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/bios16020097\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12938206\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12938206?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Shame norms, achievement pressure, and controlled self-regulation: cultural pathways to psychological distress and performance outcomes in endurance athletes.\", \"abstract\": \"Shame norms, defined as perceived group-level standards linking athletic failure to collective disgrace, represent a culturally specific but understudied antecedent of motivational regulation in Chinese competitive sport. review.alternative: Metareasoning could encompass self-correction, but the literature has prioritized efficiency (partitioning) for decades.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of significant research focus on autonomous internal consistency checking in the 1990s-2010s.

claims.statement: Traditional metareasoning focuses on the 'partition problem' of resource allocation rather than epistemic self-correction.

support.explanation: This establishes that foundational research in metareasoning is primarily about performance trade-offs, not belief truth-tracking.
support.passage: We shall introduce the metareasoning-partition problem--the problem of ideally apportioning costly reasoning resources to planning a solution versus applying resource to executing a solution to a problem.

review.alternative: Transparency does not equal autonomous self-correction; the model might expose assumptions but not reform them.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that the Equity Bias framework is purely a human-in-the-loop audit protocol with no path to automation.

claims.statement: Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible.

support.explanation: This framework suggests that identifying foundational assumptions is a design requirement for accountability, potentially providing a model for how an AI could expose its own premises.
support.passage: While traditional approaches aim to reduce or remove bias, Equity Bias instead makes bias transparent and contestable. In doing so, it broadens whose perspectives shape AI and provides a lens for understanding AI systems as interpretive agents.

actions.findings:
Traditional metareasoning focuses on the 'partition problem' of resource allocation rather than epistemic self-correction. [source-27c3e6da377b41e4]

Epistemic inclusion frameworks offer a strategy for making AI foundational assumptions 'contestable' rather than invisible. [source-443f82fd8d5543a6]
actions.limitations: Evidence remains concentrated in theoretical frameworks or external design methodologies; there is no documented empirical proof of an LLM autonomously identifying a foundational logical flaw in its own reasoning architecture and developing a superior replacement without human intervention.
actions.next_questions: Can the 'Equity Bias' framework's 'Equity Archaeology' methodology be implemented as an automated internal loop within an LLM's chain-of-thought to detect invalid premise propagation?
actions.reason: Revising the notebook to incorporate the 'Equity Bias' framework provides a clearer pathway to addressing the project's question on assumption identification.
actions.summary: AI metareasoning is currently bifurcated: established 'resource partition' models focus on computational efficiency, while emerging epistemological frameworks like 'Equity Bias' advocate for making foundational assumptions explicit and contestable. Current LLMs can support the transparency of these assumptions, but autonomous self-correction of foundational premises remains unproven.
actions.title: Foundational Constraints in AI Metareasoning

actions.question: Can an intelligent system identify a foundational assumption underlying its own reasoning, demonstrate its inadequacy, and develop a better alternative?
actions.reason: The project is now focused on the intersection of epistemic transparency (Equity Bias) and potential automation. The next step is to investigate if existing prompt-engineering or agentic-flow patterns approximate the 'Equity Archaeology' methodology.
actions.title: Meta-Reasoning and Assumption Correction
